exampleAnswers.title: Negating a Sentence Containing a Conjunction

question.text:
$\qquad$ $\mathcal{P}$ is not a rhombus and $\mathcal{Q}$ is not a rectangle.

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
question.choice1: $\mathcal{P}$ is a rhombus or $\mathcal{Q}$ is a rectangle
question.choice2: $\mathcal{P}$ is a rhombus or $\mathcal{Q}$ is not a rectangle
question.choice3: $\mathcal{P}$ is a rhombus and $\mathcal{Q}$ is not a rectangle
question.choice4: $\mathcal{P}$ is not a rhombus or $\mathcal{Q}$ is not a rectangle
question.choice5: $\mathcal{P}$ is a rhombus and $\mathcal{Q}$ is a rectangle
question.explanation:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

\[ \neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B \]

So, the negation of our statement is

\begin{align*} \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! \neg (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is not a rhombus} \textrm{ and } \mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is not a rectangle}) &\equiv \neg \big( (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is not a rhombus}) \land (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is not a rectangle}) \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \neg (\mathcal{P} \textrm{ is not a rhombus}) \lor \neg (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is not a rectangle}) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is a rhombus}) \lor (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is a rectangle}) \\[5pt] &\equiv \mathcal{P} \textrm{ is a rhombus} \textrm{ or } \mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is a rectangle}. \end{align*}

example.title: Negating a Sentence Containing a Conjunction

question.text:
$\qquad$ $\left|\{1,x\}\right|\neq 0$ and $x$ is rational

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
question.explanation:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

\[ \neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B \]

So, the negation of our statement is

\begin{align*} \neg \left(\left|\{1,x\}\right|\neq 0 \textrm{ and } x \textrm{ is rational}\right) &\equiv \neg \big( \left(\left|\{1,x\}\right|\neq 0\right) \land (x \textrm{ is rational}) \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \neg \left( \left|\{1,x\}\right|\neq 0\right) \lor \neg (x \textrm{ is rational}) \\[5pt] &\equiv \left(\left|\{1,x\}\right| = 0\right) \lor (x \textrm{ is not rational}) \\[5pt] &\equiv \left|\{1,x\}\right| = 0 \textrm{ or } x \textrm{ is not rational}. \end{align*}

\[ \neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B. \]

So, the negation of our statement is

\begin{align*} \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! \neg (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is not a rhombus} \textrm{ or } \mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is a rectangle}) &\equiv \neg \big( (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is not a rhombus}) \lor (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is a rectangle}) \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \neg (\mathcal{P} \textrm{ is not a rhombus}) \land \neg (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is a rectangle}) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\mathcal{P}\textrm{ is a rhombus}) \land (\mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is not a rectangle}) \\[5pt] &\equiv \mathcal{P} \textrm{ is a rhombus} \textrm{ and } \mathcal{Q} \textrm{ is not a rectangle}. \end{align*}

example.title: Negating a Sentence Containing a Disjunction

question.text:
$\qquad$ $10$ is odd or $10\,{|}\,50.$

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
question.explanation:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

\[ \neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B \]

So, the negation of our statement is

\begin{align*} \neg \left( 10\text{ is odd} \text{ or } 10\,{|}\,50 \right) &\equiv \neg \left( (10\text{ is odd}) \lor (10\,{|}\,50) \right) \\[5pt] &\equiv \neg \left( 10\text{ is odd} \right) \land \neg \left( 10\,{|}\,50 \right) \\[5pt] &\equiv (10\text{ is even}) \land (10 \!\not{|}\,50) \\[5pt] &\equiv 10\text{ is even} \textrm{ and } 10 \!\not{|}\,50. \end{align*}

example.title: Negating a Sentence Containing a Disjunction

question.text:
$\qquad$ $3 \, | \, 18$ or $11$ is not prime.

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
question.explanation:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

\[ \neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B. \]

So, the negation of our statement is

\begin{align*} \neg (3 \, | \, 18 \textrm{ or } 11 \textrm{ is not prime}) &\equiv \neg \big( (3 \, | \, 18) \lor (11 \textrm{ is not prime}) \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \neg ( 3 \, | \, 18) \land \neg (11 \textrm{ is not prime}) \\[5pt] &\equiv (3 \!\not{|} \, 18) \land (11 \textrm{ is prime}) \\[5pt] &\equiv 3 \!\not{|} \, 18 \textrm{ and } 11 \textrm{ is prime}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg ((Q \land P) \lor R)$ using De Morgan's laws.
question.explanation:
De Morgan's laws state that

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( Q \land P) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg R, \\[3pt] \neg ( Q \lor P) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q. \end{align*} \]

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ((Q \land P) \lor R) &\equiv \neg ( Q \land P) \land \neg R \\[3pt] &\equiv (\neg Q \lor \neg P) \land \neg R \end{align*} \]

example.title: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg (P \lor \neg Q)$ using De Morgan's laws.
question.explanation:
De Morgan's laws state that

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q, \\[3pt] \neg ( P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q. \end{align*} \]

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

\[ \begin{align*} \neg (P \lor \neg Q) &\equiv \neg P \land \neg (\neg Q) \\[3pt] &\equiv \neg P \land Q \end{align*} \]

example.title: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws

question.text: Rewrite the statement $ eg ( eg A \land ( eg B \lor A) )$ using De Morgan's laws.
question.explanation:
De Morgan's laws state that

egin{align*} eg ( A \lor B) \equiv eg A \land eg B, \[3pt] eg ( A \land B) \equiv eg A \lor eg B. \end{align*}

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

egin{align*} eg ( eg A \land ( eg B \lor A) ) &\equiv eg ( eg A) \lor eg ( eg B \lor A) \[3pt] &\equiv A \lor ( eg ( eg B) \land eg A ) \[3pt] &\equiv A \lor ( B \land eg A ) \[3pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws

question.text: Simplify the statement $\neg ( \neg A \land B )$ using De Morgan's laws.
question.explanation:
De Morgan's laws state that

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( A \land B) \equiv \neg A \lor \neg B, \\[3pt] \neg ( A \lor B) \equiv \neg A \land \neg B. \end{align*} \]

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( \neg A \land B ) &\equiv \neg ( \neg A) \lor \neg (B) \\[3pt] &\equiv A \lor \neg B \end{align*} \]

example.title: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws

question.text: Simplify the statement $ eg ( eg X \land eg Y )$ using De Morgan's laws.
question.explanation:
De Morgan's laws state that

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( X \land Y) \equiv \neg X \lor \neg Y, \\[3pt] \neg ( X \lor Y) \equiv \neg X \land \neg Y. \end{align*} \]

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

\[ \begin{align*} \neg ( \neg X \land \neg Y ) &\equiv \neg ( \neg X) \lor \neg (\neg Y) \\[3pt] &\equiv X \lor Y \end{align*} \]
